common_name: Gefner Atemoya (Nearly Self-Fruitful Popular Home Garden Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; atemoya generally needs hand pollination for reliable fruit set in US gardens, since its natural beetle pollinators are absent.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Gefner is the most widely planted atemoya cultivar for home gardens, valued for setting a reasonable crop with less hand pollination effort than most other cultivars, since it is considered nearly self-fruitful under good conditions, though hand pollination still improves fruit set and size. The rich, creamy white flesh has the classic atemoya flavor of custard, vanilla, and tropical fruit notes, and the tree bears at a relatively young age once grafted. Fruit ripens in fall and should be picked when it just begins to soften and change from green to a slightly yellow-green color, then allowed to finish ripening at room temperature indoors.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bradley is a Florida-developed atemoya cultivar valued for ripening later in the season than Gefner, extending the atemoya harvest window into late fall and helping spread out the crop for home growers with more than one tree. Like other atemoya cultivars it produces rich, custardy, sweet flesh with tropical vanilla and pineapple notes, and benefits from hand pollination for the most reliable and largest fruit set. Harvest when fruit begins to soften slightly and the skin color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. African Pride is a popular commercial and home garden atemoya cultivar known for a more compact tree size and heavy, reliable fruit production compared to some other cultivars, making it a practical choice where space is somewhat limited. The rich, sweet, custard-like flesh is classic atemoya quality, and hand pollination in the morning hours, transferring pollen from male-stage to female-stage flowers, significantly improves fruit set and size. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the skin lightens in color, then let it finish ripening at room temperature for the best eating quality.

common_name: Tango Lettuce (Frilly Deeply-Cut Green Leaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow January-February for spring or September-October for fall. Tango produces deeply frilled, ruffled, bright green leaves and is a popular cut-and-come-again variety for baby leaf and mesclun mix production.

directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Tango produces densely frilled, deeply cut, curly bright green leaves that hold up well as a cut-and-come-again crop, regrowing quickly after repeated light harvests for baby leaf salads and mesclun mixes. Its crisp, mild flavor and attractive ruffled texture make it a popular addition to mixed salad greens, and it tolerates cool weather well, making it a strong choice for both an early spring and a fall crop in zone 8-9 gardens. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head an inch above the crown to allow regrowth for a second and sometimes third harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; Sylvesta is a French Batavian-type lettuce prized for holding its crisp texture and mild flavor and resisting bolting longer than many lettuce varieties as the weather warms.

directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Sylvesta is a French Batavian-type lettuce forming loose, semi-crisp heads with a texture between soft butterhead and crunchy iceberg, valued for holding good quality and resisting premature bolting longer than many lettuce varieties as spring temperatures rise, extending the harvest window into warmer weather. The pale green leaves have a mild, sweet flavor and good crispness that holds up well in salads. Harvest as a loose head or pick outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again approach, and provide light afternoon shade in the warmest part of the season to further extend its quality.
